evidence: createApp only registers Express routes, and each handler passes its work to CatalogueService or OrderService methods
asObject/requireString/requireNumber/param only check the shape of request input, which is transport work
statusFor and errorHandler turn DomainError subclasses into HTTP status codes and JSON error bodies, which is transport work
/stock handler only selects and renames fields from catalogue.listProducts() for the response; it makes no business decisions
POST /orders/:id/pay etc. call orders.transition(id, 'paid'); the domain still decides whether the move is valid (InvalidTransitionError)
parsedVerdict.reasoning:
src/infrastructure/http.ts passes. It is an Express HTTP adapter, and everything it does is transport work. That fits the infrastructure layer, since the model has no separate presentation layer.

What the file does:
- Sets up routes.
- Checks the shape of request bodies and path parameters (asObject, requireString, requireNumber, param).
- Turns a request into a call to the application services (catalogue.addProduct, orders.placeOrder, orders.transition, orders.advance, orders.cancel).
- Shapes responses, such as the /stock view, which only renames and selects fields.
- Turns errors into HTTP status codes (statusFor, errorHandler).

What it does not do: it holds no business rules. Stock rules, order state-machine rules and pricing are all left to the application and domain services. The shortcut routes (/pay, /pack, /ship, /deliver) only give a URL a fixed target state; whether the move is allowed is still checked downstream (InvalidTransitionError comes from the domain). The isOrderState check only validates input against the list of valid states from the domain. It does not decide which transitions are allowed.

There is no persistence logic and no use-case orchestration in the file.
